description: Swiss Chard is a leafy green vegetable in the Beet family. The thick stems come in a variety of colors including white, pink, red, yellow, orange, and pale green. It has large, crinkly leaves with distinctive veins. The leaves and stems are edible and high in nutrients. Swiss chard can be eaten raw or sautéed, baked, or steamed.
sowing_method: Direct seed indoors or outdoors. Transplant seedlings after hardening off.

growing_information.text: One of the best of the pot-herbs, though not so generally known, is the chard or leaf-beet, which usually requires the whole season to mature, although it will give a succession of leaves from early summer until fall. The leaf-blades and midribs of the chard are very broad, and are usually white or slightly tinted, instead of green. Gardeners often blanch them further by tying the leaves together while growing. The seeds are sown in the spring as thickly as the ordinary beet is sown, and the plants are thinned until they stand six to twelve inches apart in the row.

Swiss chard, also known as leaf-beet, is a valuable plant that should be cultivated more extensively. It requires the whole growing season to mature but will provide a succession of leaves from early summer until fall. The part eaten is not the root, but the midrib of the leaf which is prepared much like asparagus and has a distinct flavor from beetroot. To grow Swiss chard, sow seeds in the spring as thickly as ordinary beets are sown, about 1cm (0.4in) deep, and thin the plants until they stand 15-30cm (6-12in) apart in rows that are spaced 90cm to 1.2m (3ft to 4ft) apart. The soil should be richer than for ordinary beets. Covering with straw in the fall will aid early growth and help blanch the stems. Gardeners often further blanch the leaves by tying them together while growing. Swiss chard is a very valuable plant and should be cultivated more extensively.
